grep: Searches for specific patterns or text strings within files and outputs matching lines.
cd: Changes the current working directory in the command-line interface.
wget: A non-interactive network downloader used to retrieve files from the web via HTTP, HTTPS, and FTP.
curl: A command-line tool for transferring data to or from a server using various protocols like HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, etc.
nat: Network Address Translation maps IP addresses in a packet header while in transit across a routing device.
ls: Lists directory contents, showing files and folders inside the current working directory.
pwd: Prints the absolute path of the current working directory.
mkdir: Creates a new directory or folder at the specified location.
chmod: Changes file or directory access permissions in Unix-like operating systems.
chown: Changes the user and group ownership of file system files and directories.
ssh: Secure Shell protocol for secure remote login and other secure network services over an insecure network.
iptables: A user-space application program that allows a system administrator to configure the IP packet filter rules of the Linux kernel firewall.
systemctl: A command-line tool to inspect and manage the systemd system and service manager.
ping: Tests the reachability of a host across an Internet Protocol network and measures round-trip time.
ipconfig: A Windows utility used to display all current TCP/IP network configuration values and refresh DHCP and DNS settings.
powershell: A task automation and configuration management framework from Microsoft, consisting of a powerful shell and scripting language.
cmd: The command-line interpreter application on Windows operating systems.
registry: A hierarchical database that stores low-level settings for the Microsoft Windows operating system and for applications.
active-directory: A Microsoft directory service that manages permissions and access to network resources in a Windows Domain environment.
snat: Source Network Address Translation modifies the source IP address in the IP header of outbound packets, commonly used for sharing a single public IP.
dnat: Destination Network Address Translation modifies the destination IP address of incoming packets, often used for port forwarding.
pat: Port Address Translation (or NAT overload) maps multiple private IP addresses to a single public IP address using different ports.
subnet: A logical subdivision of an IP network, allowing a network to be partitioned into smaller, manageable segments.
vlan: Virtual Local Area Network partitions a physical network into multiple logical networks for security and traffic management.
dhcp: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol automatically assigns IP addresses and network configuration parameters to devices on a network.
dns: Domain Name System translates human-friendly domain names into machine-readable IP addresses.
firewall: A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules.
ldap: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol used for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services over an IP network.
raid: Redundant Array of Independent Disks data storage virtualization technology that combines multiple physical disk drive components into one or more logical units for redundancy or performance.
hypervisor: Software, firmware, or hardware that creates and runs virtual machines (e.g., VMware, Hyper-V, KVM).
ansible: An open-source software provisioning, configuration management, and application-deployment tool using infrastructure as code.
kubernetes: An open-source container orchestration system for automating software deployment, scaling, and management.
tcp: Transmission Control Protocol: a connection-oriented transport protocol that provides reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of a stream of bytes between applications.
udp: User Datagram Protocol: a connectionless transport protocol that sends datagrams without guarantees of delivery, ordering, or duplicate protection.
icmp: Internet Control Message Protocol: used by network devices to send error messages and operational information (e.g., ping).
icmpv6: ICMP for IPv6: carries error and informational messages for IPv6, and is essential for Neighbor Discovery and SLAAC.
arp: Address Resolution Protocol: maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on a local network segment.
ndp: Neighbor Discovery Protocol: the IPv6 equivalent of ARP plus router discovery, using ICMPv6 messages.
http: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the application-layer protocol used for transmitting web pages and other resources.
https: HTTP Secure: HTTP layered over TLS, providing encryption and authentication between client and server.
tls: Transport Layer Security: cryptographic protocol that provides secure communication over a network; successor to SSL.
ssl: Secure Sockets Layer: the deprecated predecessor to TLS. Should not be used for new deployments.
ftp: File Transfer Protocol: a standard network protocol used for transferring files between a client and server on a computer network.
sftp: SSH File Transfer Protocol: a secure file transfer protocol that runs over SSH, unlike plain FTP.
scp: Secure Copy Protocol: a means of securely transferring files between a local and remote host over SSH.
rsync: A utility for efficiently transferring and synchronizing files across systems by only copying the differences.
smtp: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: the standard protocol for sending email between servers.
imap: Internet Message Access Protocol: a protocol for retrieving email from a server while keeping it on the server.
pop3: Post Office Protocol version 3: an older email retrieval protocol that typically downloads and deletes messages from the server.
bgp: Border Gateway Protocol: the routing protocol that exchanges routing information between autonomous systems on the internet.
ospf: Open Shortest Path First: a link-state interior gateway routing protocol for IP networks.
rip: Routing Information Protocol: a distance-vector routing protocol that uses hop count as its metric.
mpls: Multiprotocol Label Switching: a routing technique that directs data based on short path labels rather than long network addresses.
vpn: Virtual Private Network: extends a private network across a public one, providing encryption and anonymity.
ipsec: Internet Protocol Security: a suite of protocols for authenticating and encrypting IP packets, often used in VPNs.
wireguard: A modern, high-performance VPN protocol built into the Linux kernel.
openvpn: An open-source VPN implementation using SSL/TLS for key exchange.
mtu: Maximum Transmission Unit: the largest packet size that can be transmitted over a network link without fragmentation.
ttl: Time To Live: a field in IP packets that is decremented at each hop; when it reaches zero the packet is dropped.
cidr: Classless Inter-Domain Routing: a method for allocating IP addresses and routing that uses variable-length subnet masks.
subnet mask: A 32-bit number that separates the network portion of an IP address from the host portion.
mac address: Media Access Control address: a unique 48-bit identifier assigned to a network interface controller.
eui-64: Extended Unique Identifier: a 64-bit identifier derived from a MAC address, used to form the interface identifier of an IPv6 address.
loopback: A special network address (127.0.0.1 in IPv4, ::1 in IPv6) that refers to the local machine.
multicast: A one-to-many communication pattern where data is sent to a group of interested receivers.
anycast: A one-to-nearest communication pattern where data is delivered to the topologically closest member of a group.
unicast: A one-to-one communication pattern where data is sent to a single destination.
broadcast: A one-to-all communication pattern in a network segment. IPv6 has no broadcast; it uses multicast instead.
ethernet: The dominant family of wired LAN technologies, defined by IEEE 802.3, carrying frames over twisted pair, coax, or fiber.
osi model: A conceptual framework that standardizes network communication into seven layers, from physical media to applications.
tcp/ip model: A four-layer networking model (Link, Internet, Transport, Application) that underlies the modern internet.
latency: The time delay between sending a request and receiving a response, typically measured in milliseconds.
bandwidth: The maximum rate of data transfer across a network path, typically measured in bits per second.
throughput: The actual rate of successful data delivery over a network, often lower than the theoretical bandwidth.
packet: A formatted unit of data carried by a packet-switched network, containing headers and a payload.
frame: A data unit at the link layer, encapsulating a packet with link-layer addressing and error checking.
port: A 16-bit number identifying a specific process or service on a host, used with TCP or UDP.
port forwarding: A NAT technique that redirects incoming traffic on a specific port to a host inside a private network.
dmz: Demilitarized Zone: a subnetwork that exposes external-facing services to an untrusted network while isolating the internal network.
proxy: An intermediary server that forwards requests between clients and other servers.
reverse proxy: A proxy that sits in front of servers and forwards client requests to them, often for load balancing or TLS termination.
load balancer: A device or service that distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers.
cdn: Content Delivery Network: a geographically distributed network of servers that delivers content closer to users.
acl: Access Control List: a list of rules that specify which users or systems are granted or denied access to a resource.
aaa: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting: the three pillars of access control in networking and security.
tls handshake: The initial negotiation in a TLS session where client and server agree on cipher suites and exchange keys.
certificate: A digital document that binds a public key to an identity, signed by a certificate authority.
ca: Certificate Authority: a trusted entity that issues digital certificates.
pki: Public Key Infrastructure: the set of roles, policies, and procedures needed to create, manage, and revoke digital certificates.
hash: A fixed-size value computed from input data, used for integrity checks and password storage.
encryption: The process of encoding information so that only authorized parties can access it.
symmetric encryption: Encryption using the same key for both encryption and decryption.
asymmetric encryption: Encryption using a pair of keys: one public for encryption, one private for decryption.
public key: A cryptographic key that can be shared openly and is used to encrypt data or verify signatures.
private key: A cryptographic key kept secret by its owner, used to decrypt data or create signatures.
digital signature: A mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity and integrity of a message.
ssh key: A cryptographic key pair used to authenticate to SSH servers instead of a password.
gpg: GNU Privacy Guard: a free implementation of the OpenPGP standard for encryption and signing.
openssl: A widely used toolkit for TLS/SSL and general-purpose cryptography.
linux: A free and open-source Unix-like operating system kernel first released by Linus Torvalds in 1991.
unix: A family of multitasking, multiuser operating systems originally developed at Bell Labs in the 1970s.
kernel: The core of an operating system that manages hardware, memory, processes, and system calls.
shell: A command-line interpreter that provides an interface for users to interact with the operating system.
bash: Bourne Again Shell: the default shell on most Linux distributions and macOS.
zsh: Z shell: an extended Bourne shell with many improvements, popular as an interactive shell.
fish: Friendly Interactive Shell: a user-friendly shell with syntax highlighting and autosuggestions.
environment variable: A named value in a process's environment, used to configure programs at runtime.
path: The environment variable listing directories searched for executable commands.
alias: A shell shortcut that expands to a longer command.
pipe: A shell operator (|) that sends the output of one command as input to another.
redirect: A shell operator that sends command output to a file or device instead of the terminal.
glob: A pattern-matching syntax in shells using wildcards like * and ? to match filenames.
stdin: Standard input: the default input stream for a process, usually the terminal.
stdout: Standard output: the default output stream for a process, usually the terminal.
stderr: Standard error: the stream where a process writes error messages, separate from stdout.
exit code: A number returned by a process to indicate success (0) or failure (non-zero).
sudo: A program that allows a permitted user to execute a command as another user, typically root.
root: The superuser account on Unix-like systems with unrestricted access to the system.
user: A user account on a multi-user operating system, identified by a username and a numeric UID.
group: A collection of users in Unix-like systems, used to grant shared permissions.
permission: An access right on a file or directory, specifying read, write, and execute for user, group, and others.
umask: A value that determines the default permissions for newly created files and directories.
file system: The structure and rules an operating system uses to store and retrieve files on a storage device.
mount: The act of making a file system accessible at a directory in the operating system's tree.
partition: A logical division of a storage device that can hold a file system.
inode: A data structure on Unix-like file systems that stores metadata about a file (not its name).
symlink: A symbolic link: a special file that points to another file or directory.
hard link: A directory entry that points to the same inode as another file, effectively a second name for the same data.
tmpfs: A temporary file system stored in memory (RAM) rather than on persistent storage.
swap: Disk space used as virtual memory when physical RAM is exhausted.
daemon: A background process that runs without a controlling terminal, often providing a service.
process: A running instance of a program, with its own memory, file descriptors, and PID.
pid: Process ID: a numeric identifier assigned to each running process.
signal: A software interrupt delivered to a process to notify it of an event (e.g., SIGTERM, SIGKILL).
job: A process or pipeline managed by a shell's job control system.
cron: A time-based job scheduler on Unix-like systems that runs commands at specified intervals.
systemd: A modern init system and service manager used by most Linux distributions.
systemctl: A command-line tool to inspect and manage the systemd system and service manager.
journalctl: A command-line tool to view logs collected by the systemd journal.
unit: A systemd configuration file describing a service, socket, device, mount, or other resource.
init: The first process started by the kernel on a Unix-like system, responsible for starting other processes.
init system: The software that initializes the system after the kernel boots and manages services.
bootloader: A program that loads the operating system kernel into memory at boot time.
grub: GRand Unified Bootloader: a widely used bootloader for Linux and other operating systems.
uefi: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface: the modern firmware interface that replaced legacy BIOS.
bios: Basic Input/Output System: the legacy firmware interface on older PCs.
mbr: Master Boot Record: the first sector of a disk in legacy BIOS booting, containing the bootloader stub and partition table.
gpt: GUID Partition Table: the modern partition table format used with UEFI, supporting disks larger than 2 TB.
lvm: Logical Volume Manager: a system for managing disk storage by abstracting physical volumes into logical ones.
filesystem hierarchy: The standardized directory layout on Unix-like systems (e.g., /etc, /usr, /var).
pacman: The package manager for Arch Linux, used to install, update, and remove software.
aur: Arch User Repository: a community-driven repository of PKGBUILD files for Arch Linux.
pkgbuild: A shell script that describes how to build a package from source, used by makepkg.
makepkg: A script that automates building packages from PKGBUILDs on Arch Linux.
yay: Yet Another Yogurt: a popular AUR helper for Arch Linux written in Go.
paru: A feature-rich AUR helper for Arch Linux written in Rust.
reflector: A tool that retrieves and sorts Arch Linux mirror lists by speed and freshness.
base-devel: A package group on Arch Linux that provides essential tools for building packages from source.
arch wiki: The community-maintained documentation wiki for Arch Linux, widely used across Linux distributions.
apt: The package manager used on Debian and Ubuntu systems.
dpkg: The low-level package manager underlying apt on Debian-based systems.
yum: The legacy package manager for RPM-based distributions, superseded by dnf.
dnf: The modern package manager for Fedora and other RPM-based distributions.
rpm: RPM Package Manager: a package format and tool used by Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE.
snap: A universal package format developed by Canonical for Linux.
flatpak: A universal package format for Linux with sandboxing and per-app dependencies.
appimage: A portable Linux application format that runs without installation.
docker: A platform for building, distributing, and running containers.
container: A lightweight, isolated user-space environment sharing the host kernel.
image: A read-only template used to create containers, containing the application and its dependencies.
dockerfile: A text file with instructions for building a Docker image.
docker compose: A tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file.
podman: A daemonless container engine compatible with Docker, popular on RHEL and Fedora.
lxc: Linux Containers: an OS-level virtualization method for running isolated Linux systems.
lxd: A container hypervisor built on LXC, providing a REST API and image management.
namespace: A Linux kernel feature that isolates process views of system resources (PID, net, mount, etc.).
cgroup: Control Group: a Linux kernel feature that limits, accounts for, and isolates resource usage of processes.
kubernetes: An open-source container orchestration system for automating software deployment, scaling, and management.
kubectl: The command-line tool for interacting with a Kubernetes cluster.
helm: A package manager for Kubernetes that uses charts to define applications.
pod: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, containing one or more containers.
node: A worker machine in a Kubernetes cluster that runs pods.
cluster: A set of machines working together, often under an orchestrator like Kubernetes.
istio: A service mesh for Kubernetes providing traffic management, security, and observability.
terraform: An infrastructure-as-code tool by HashiCorp for provisioning cloud resources.
ansible: An open-source software provisioning, configuration management, and application-deployment tool using infrastructure as code.
puppet: A configuration management tool for automating infrastructure.
chef: A configuration management tool for automating infrastructure.
vagrant: A tool for building and managing portable virtual development environments.
virtualbox: A free and open-source hypervisor by Oracle for running virtual machines.
vmware: A commercial virtualization platform for running virtual machines.
kvm: Kernel-based Virtual Machine: a Linux kernel module that turns the kernel into a hypervisor.
qemu: A generic and open-source machine emulator and virtualizer.
hypervisor: Software, firmware, or hardware that creates and runs virtual machines (e.g., VMware, Hyper-V, KVM).
cloud: On-demand computing resources delivered over the internet, billed by usage.
aws: Amazon Web Services: the largest public cloud provider.
gcp: Google Cloud Platform: Google's public cloud offering.
vps: Virtual Private Server: a virtual machine sold as a service by hosting providers.
serverless: A cloud execution model where the provider manages servers and scales automatically.
lambda: AWS Lambda: a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events.
object storage: A storage architecture that manages data as objects, used by S3, GCS, and Azure Blob.
s3: Amazon Simple Storage Service: an object storage service from AWS.
load balancing: The distribution of network or application traffic across multiple servers.
autoscaling: The automatic adjustment of compute resources based on demand.
ci/cd: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment: practices for automating software build, test, and release.
github actions: A CI/CD platform built into GitHub for automating workflows.
gitlab ci: GitLab's built-in continuous integration and delivery system.
jenkins: An open-source automation server used for CI/CD.
pipeline: A sequence of automated steps for building, testing, and deploying software.
firewall: A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules.
ids: Intrusion Detection System: monitors network or system activity for malicious behavior.
ips: Intrusion Prevention System: like IDS but can also block detected threats.
siem: Security Information and Event Management: a system that aggregates and analyzes security events.
soc: Security Operations Center: a team and facility responsible for monitoring and responding to security incidents.
zero trust: A security model that assumes no implicit trust and verifies every request.
mfa: Multi-Factor Authentication: requires two or more verification factors to grant access.
2fa: Two-Factor Authentication: a subset of MFA using exactly two factors.
totp: Time-based One-Time Password: an algorithm for generating short-lived authentication codes.
oauth: An open standard for access delegation, commonly used for 'Sign in with...' flows.
oidc: OpenID Connect: an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0.
saml: Security Assertion Markup Language: an XML-based standard for exchanging authentication and authorization data.
jwt: JSON Web Token: a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims between two parties.
rbac: Role-Based Access Control: an access control model where permissions are assigned to roles, and roles to users.
abac: Attribute-Based Access Control: an access control model based on attributes of the subject, object, and environment.
penetration test: An authorized simulated cyberattack on a system to evaluate its security.
vulnerability: A weakness in a system that can be exploited to compromise its security.
cve: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a public catalog of known security vulnerabilities.
exploit: A piece of software or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability.
malware: Software designed to harm, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to a system.
ransomware: Malware that encrypts a victim's data and demands payment for decryption.
phishing: A social engineering attack that tricks users into revealing sensitive information.
ddos: Distributed Denial of Service: an attack that floods a target with traffic from many sources.
mitm: Man-in-the-Middle: an attack where the attacker secretly relays or alters communication between two parties.
xss: Cross-Site Scripting: a vulnerability where attacker-controlled scripts run in a victim's browser.
sql injection: A code injection attack that inserts malicious SQL into input fields to manipulate a database.
csrf: Cross-Site Request Forgery: an attack that tricks a logged-in user's browser into making unwanted requests.
rate limiting: A technique that limits how often an action can be performed in a given time window.
honeypot: A decoy system designed to attract attackers and observe their behavior.
red team: A group that simulates attacks to test an organization's defenses.
blue team: A group responsible for defending against attacks and responding to incidents.
purple team: A collaborative approach that combines red and blue team activities.
json: JavaScript Object Notation: a lightweight data-interchange format that is easy for humans to read and machines to parse.
yaml: YAML Ain't Markup Language: a human-readable data serialization format often used for configuration.
xml: Extensible Markup Language: a markup language for encoding documents in a format readable by both humans and machines.
toml: Tom's Obvious Minimal Language: a configuration file format designed to be easy to read.
csv: Comma-Separated Values: a simple file format for tabular data.
markdown: A lightweight markup language for formatting plain text, used for documentation and READMEs.
html: HyperText Markup Language: the standard markup language for documents displayed in a web browser.
css: Cascading Style Sheets: a stylesheet language used to describe the presentation of HTML documents.
javascript: A high-level, interpreted programming language primarily used for interactive web pages.
typescript: A typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript.
python: A high-level, interpreted programming language known for readability and a large ecosystem.
go: A statically typed, compiled programming language developed at Google.
rust: A systems programming language focused on memory safety and performance.
c: A general-purpose, procedural programming language, foundational for Unix and Linux.
c++: A general-purpose programming language with object-oriented and low-level features.
java: A high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language that runs on the JVM.
node.js: A runtime for executing JavaScript outside the browser, built on Chrome's V8 engine.
npm: The default package manager for Node.js.
cargo: The package manager and build system for Rust.
go modules: The dependency management system for Go.
maven: A build automation tool primarily for Java projects.
gradle: A build automation tool for multi-language software development, popular in Android and Java.
make: A build automation tool that reads a Makefile to determine how to compile a project.
cmake: A cross-platform build-system generator used for C and C++ projects.
compiler: A program that translates source code into machine code or another language.
interpreter: A program that executes source code directly without compiling it to machine code first.
linker: A program that combines object files into a single executable or library.
linter: A tool that analyzes source code for stylistic or programmatic errors.
debugger: A tool that allows a developer to inspect and control the execution of a program.
ide: Integrated Development Environment: software that combines editing, building, and debugging tools.
editor: A program for editing text files. Common examples: vim, emacs, nano, VS Code.
vim: A highly configurable modal text editor, ubiquitous on Unix-like systems.
neovim: A modern fork of Vim with improved extensibility and async support.
emacs: A highly extensible, self-documenting text editor.
nano: A simple terminal-based text editor, often preinstalled on Linux.
vs code: Visual Studio Code: a popular source-code editor by Microsoft.
regex: Regular Expression: a sequence of characters that specifies a search pattern.
utf-8: A variable-width character encoding capable of encoding all Unicode code points.
unicode: A character encoding standard that assigns a unique number to every character in most of the world's writing systems.
ascii: A 7-bit character encoding standard for English letters, digits, and punctuation.
base64: A binary-to-text encoding that represents binary data using 64 printable ASCII characters.
uuid: Universally Unique Identifier: a 128-bit label used to uniquely identify information.
hash function: A function that maps data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size value.
sha-256: A cryptographic hash function producing a 256-bit digest, widely used for integrity checks.
md5: A widely used but cryptographically broken hash function producing a 128-bit digest.
checksum: A value computed from data to detect errors introduced during storage or transmission.
api: Application Programming Interface: a set of rules and definitions that allows software to communicate.
rest: Representational State Transfer: an architectural style for distributed systems, common in web APIs.
graphql: A query language and runtime for APIs that lets clients request exactly the data they need.
grpc: A high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.
websocket: A protocol providing full-duplex communication over a single TCP connection, often used for real-time web apps.
webhook: A user-defined HTTP callback triggered by an event.
cors: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: a browser security mechanism that controls which origins can access a resource.
cookie: A small piece of data stored by a browser and sent with requests to the same origin.
session: A server-side mechanism for tracking a user's state across multiple requests.
cache: A temporary storage layer that speeds up access to frequently used data.
cdn: Content Delivery Network: a geographically distributed network of servers that delivers content closer to users.
dns record: An entry in a DNS zone file, such as A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, or TXT, that maps names to values.
a record: A DNS record that maps a domain name to an IPv4 address.
aaaa record: A DNS record that maps a domain name to an IPv6 address.
cname: Canonical Name record: a DNS record that aliases one domain name to another.
mx record: Mail Exchange record: a DNS record that specifies the mail servers for a domain.
txt record: A DNS record that holds arbitrary text, commonly used for SPF, DKIM, and domain verification.
spf: Sender Policy Framework: a DNS TXT record that lists servers authorized to send email for a domain.
dkim: DomainKeys Identified Mail: a method for signing email to verify authenticity.
dmarc: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance: a policy that builds on SPF and DKIM to protect against email spoofing.
IPv4: Internet Protocol version 4: the fourth version of the Internet Protocol, using 32-bit addresses written in dotted-decimal notation (e.g., 192.168.1.1). Still the most widely deployed addressing scheme.
IPv6: Internet Protocol version 6: the successor to IPv4, using 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal groups separated by colons. Designed to eliminate address exhaustion and restore end-to-end connectivity.
KRITIS: Kritische Infrastrukturen: organizations and facilities of vital importance to the state and society. If they fail or are impaired, it can lead to supply shortages or significant disruptions to public safety [citation:3][citation:17].
Binär: Binary: a number system using only two digits, 0 and 1. It is the foundation of computing because electronic components can easily represent two states (on/off, true/false) [citation:4][citation:11][citation:18].
Bit: The smallest unit of information in computing, representing a single binary value: 0 or 1.
Byte: A unit of digital information consisting of 8 bits. Commonly used to measure file sizes and memory.
Dualsystem: The binary number system (base-2), using only 0 and 1. Also called the Binärsystem [citation:11][citation:18].
API: Application Programming Interface: a set of defined rules and protocols that allows different software systems to communicate with each other. Central to modern system integration [citation:8].
Middleware: Software that acts as a bridge between different applications or systems, enabling them to communicate and exchange data without direct point-to-point connections.
Punkt-zu-Punkt-Integration: Point-to-point integration: directly connecting two systems. Simple for a few connections but grows exponentially in complexity as systems are added [citation:1][citation:8].
Hub-and-Spoke: An integration model where every system connects to a single central hub that mediates requests and separates senders from receivers [citation:1].
ESB: Enterprise Service Bus: a centralized integration layer that allows different applications to communicate through a common messaging backbone [citation:1].
EDI: Electronic Data Interchange: a standardized format for exchanging business documents (orders, invoices, etc.) between organizations [citation:8].
B2B-Integration: Business-to-Business integration: connecting systems and processes between different companies or trading partners, often using EDI standards [citation:8].
ETL: Extract, Transform, Load: a process for extracting data from source systems, transforming it into a consistent format, and loading it into a target repository [citation:8].
Datenschnittstelle: Data interface: a defined point of interaction where two systems exchange data, governed by a specific protocol or format.
Systemintegration: System integration: the process of linking different IT systems and software applications so they function as a unified whole [citation:8].
Lastenheft: Requirements specification: a document describing all requirements from the customer's perspective for a system to be built or integrated [citation:14].
Pflichtenheft: Technical specification: a document describing how the requirements from the Lastenheft will be technically implemented from the contractor's perspective [citation:14].
BSI: Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik: the German Federal Office for Information Security, responsible for cybersecurity and KRITIS oversight [citation:6][citation:17].
BSI-Kritisverordnung: The German regulation defining which facilities and threshold values qualify as critical infrastructure under the BSI Act [citation:19].
Sektoren: Sectors: the categories of critical infrastructure defined by law, including Energy, Health, IT and Telecommunications, Transport, Water, Finance, Food, and Waste Disposal [citation:17].
Schwellenwert: Threshold value: the minimum capacity or service level at which a facility becomes classified as critical infrastructure under the Kritisverordnung [citation:5][citation:19].
IT-System: IT system: a combination of hardware, software, and network components that together perform a specific function or set of functions.
Client-Server: A network architecture where clients request services and servers provide them. The basis for most modern network applications [citation:14].
Server: A computer or program that provides services, data, or resources to other computers (clients) over a network [citation:14].
Client: A computer or program that requests and uses services or resources provided by a server [citation:14].
Netzwerktopologie: Network topology: the physical or logical arrangement of devices and connections in a network (e.g., star, ring, bus, mesh) [citation:14].
LAN: Local Area Network: a network covering a small geographic area, such as a single building or campus.
WAN: Wide Area Network: a network covering a large geographic area, often connecting multiple LANs across cities or countries.
VLAN: Virtual Local Area Network: a logical partition of a physical network, allowing separate broadcast domains for security and traffic management.
Subnetz: Subnet: a logical subdivision of an IP network, allowing a network to be partitioned into smaller, manageable segments.
Gateway: A network node that serves as an entry point from one network to another, often translating between different protocols or addressing schemes.
Router: A network device that forwards data packets between computer networks, determining the best path based on routing tables.
Switch: A network device that connects devices within a LAN, forwarding data only to the port where the destination device is connected.
Firewall: A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on predetermined security rules.
VPN: Virtual Private Network: extends a private network across a public one, providing encryption and secure remote access.
Backup: A copy of data stored separately so it can be restored if the original is lost or corrupted [citation:6].
Redundanz: Redundancy: the duplication of critical components or functions to increase reliability, ensuring continued operation if one part fails.
Ausfallsicherheit: Failure safety: the ability of a system to continue operating or recover gracefully when components fail.
Skalierbarkeit: Scalability: the ability of a system to handle a growing amount of work by adding resources.
Interoperabilität: Interoperability: the ability of different systems, devices, or applications to exchange and make use of information.
Standardisierung: Standardization: the process of implementing and developing technical standards to ensure compatibility and consistency across systems.
